title: Monitor and control implementation of work site insecticide, herbicide and fungicide interventions

lessons.title: Supervising application on site
lessons.html:
The supervisor's role

At NQF level 5 the pest management officer is often responsible not only for applying products but for supervising a team and controlling the quality and safety of the whole intervention. Monitoring and control means checking, during the work, that what is happening matches the plan, the label and the law, and correcting deviations immediately.

What to monitor during application

  • Correct area: only the planned treatment zones are treated; boundaries, buffer zones and exclusions are respected.
  • Correct product and rate: the mix matches the calculated dose; team members are not adding extra product.
  • Correct technique: appropriate nozzle, pressure, walking speed and distance from target; crack and crevice placement rather than broadcast spraying where planned.
  • Coverage: uniform, without missed strips or excessive run-off. Spray dye, where used, helps check herbicide coverage.
  • Weather: wind, temperature and rain risk for outdoor work; stop if conditions change.
  • Safety: PPE worn correctly, no eating, drinking or smoking, no unauthorised persons entering.
  • Environment: no drift towards water, crops, gardens or hives; no spills at mixing sites.

Controlling deviations

DeviationControl action
Wind picks up and drift is visibleStop spraying; resume only when conditions are suitable
Person enters treated areaStop work, remove the person safely, check for exposure, reinforce barriers
Wrong nozzle or pressureStop, correct and recheck calibration
Worker not wearing PPEStop that worker until PPE is correct
SpillStop, contain, clean up per SDS, report

Communication

Keep in contact with team members by sight or radio. Agree simple stop signals. Inform the client contact of progress and of any incidents.

lessons.title: Checking effectiveness and handling problems
lessons.html:
Has the intervention worked?

Effectiveness is checked at planned intervals after treatment, against the objective set in the plan.

Methods of evaluation

  • Insecticide treatments: sticky monitor counts, visual inspections at night or early morning, client sighting logs, bait consumption.
  • Rodent programmes: bait take, trap catches, fresh droppings and tracking dust.
  • Herbicide treatments: percentage kill of target plants at the time the label indicates effects should be visible; regrowth and seedling emergence at follow-up.
  • Fungicide treatments: disease incidence and severity on treated plants or timber compared with before treatment.

Typical timelines

Gel baits may take days to reduce cockroach numbers; systemic herbicides may take one to several weeks to show full effect; residual sprays decline over time. Do not judge too soon, but do not wait too long to act if results are poor.

Investigating failure

  1. Confirm the identification was correct.
  2. Check records: right product, dose, coverage and placement?
  3. Check conditions: rain soon after application, dusty plants, cleaning that removed residues, temperature.
  4. Check whether client actions were done: sanitation, proofing, removal of harbourage.
  5. Consider re-infestation from neighbouring areas.
  6. Consider resistance, especially after repeated use of one chemical group.

Corrective actions

Agree and record corrective actions: re-treatment with a different mode of action, improved placement, more client sanitation, proofing, more frequent monitoring or a different strategy entirely. Re-treat only within label limits on the number and interval of applications.

lessons.title: Records, incidents and closure
lessons.html:
Records of implementation

Complete, accurate records show that the work was done correctly and are required by clients, auditors and inspectors.

  • Application record: date and time, site and areas treated, target pest, product name and registration number, batch number, amount of concentrate and total mix, application method and equipment, weather for outdoor work, operator names and registration.
  • Stock reconciliation: product issued from stock, product used and product returned must agree.
  • Monitoring results: counts and observations at each evaluation visit.
  • Client communication: service report given, precautions explained, re-entry advised.

Incident management

Any spill, exposure, complaint of illness, damage to non-target plants or animals, or contamination of food or water must be:

  1. Responded to immediately to protect people and the environment.
  2. Reported to your manager and to the client.
  3. Investigated to find the root cause.
  4. Recorded with corrective and preventive actions.

For anyone exposed, follow the label and SDS first aid instructions, and get medical help with the label. First aid must be performed by people with hands-on training from an accredited provider.

Closing the intervention

  • Remove notices and barriers only when the re-entry period has passed.
  • Ensure equipment is cleaned and stored, and waste and containers are secured for correct disposal.
  • Hand over to the client with a written report including results, outstanding client actions and the next monitoring date.
  • Review with the team what went well and what can be improved.

Key points

  • Monitor area, product and rate, technique, coverage, weather, safety and environment during application.
  • Stop work and correct deviations such as drift, missing PPE, wrong equipment or unauthorised entry.
  • Evaluate effectiveness against the plan objective using suitable methods and timelines.
  • Investigate failures systematically before re-treating within label limits.
  • Keep full application, stock, monitoring and incident records, and close out with a client report.
